value.question: What does NASA mean by systems engineering, and what broad activities does the discipline cover?

steps.description: Search the NASA corpus for NASA's definition of systems engineering and the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook description of the discipline's scope
Find current NASA sources (e.g., NASA SE Handbook, NPR 7123.1) confirming the definition and broad activities systems engineering covers

key_findings: NASA's own definition, stated in the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook, is that "at NASA, 'systems engineering' is defined as a methodical, multi-disciplinary approach for the design, realization, technical management, operations, and retirement of a system," with a "system" being "the combination of elements that function together to produce the capability required to meet a need," including "all hardware, software, equipment, facilities, personnel, processes, and procedures needed for this purpose" (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p12-chunk-32).

The handbook characterizes the discipline qualitatively as "the art and science of developing an operable system capable of meeting requirements within often opposed constraints" and as "a holistic, integrative discipline" in which the contributions of structural, electrical, mechanism, power, human factors and many other engineers "are evaluated and balanced, one against another, to produce a coherent whole that is not dominated by the perspective of a single discipline" (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p13-chunk-34).

The broad activities covered span the full system life cycle — design, realization, technical management, operations and retirement — and are expressed in the handbook through life-cycle phase descriptions such as Phase A ("Develop final mission concept, system-level requirements, needed system technology developments, and program/project technical management plans") and Phase B ("Preliminary Design and Technology Completion") (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p19-chunk-57, nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p12-chunk-32).

Systems engineering is described as crosscutting and tradeoff-driven: "Systems engineering is about tradeoffs and compromises; it uses a broad crosscutting view of the system rather than a single discipline view," the systems engineer being "skilled in the art and science of balancing organizational, cost, and technical interactions in complex systems" and supporting Program and Project Planning and Control (PP&C) with cost and schedule information (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p14-chunk-38). The handbook itself is offered as "a generic description of Systems Engineering (SE) as it should be applied throughout NASA" and as a companion for implementing NPR 7123.1 (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p11-chunk-28, nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p10-chunk-27).
gaps: No verbatim definition or scope statement from NPR 7123.1 itself is in the evidence; NPR 7123.1 is referenced only as the requirements document the handbook accompanies (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p11-chunk-28), so the authoritative regulatory wording remains unconfirmed.

The evidence does not enumerate the handbook's/NPR 7123.1's structured set of common technical processes (e.g., system design, product realization, technical management process groups, or the "SE engine"), so the full taxonomy of broad activities is only partially established from life-cycle phases and prose descriptions.

Activity coverage is uneven: design, technical management and preliminary design/concept phases are documented (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p19-chunk-57, nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p14-chunk-38), but operations, retirement, and crosscutting technical activities such as verification/validation, interfaces, and configuration management are not elaborated in the recorded excerpts.

All evidence comes from the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook; no independent current NASA web sources (e.g., NASA SE Handbook landing page or NPR 7123.1 text) were captured, and no evidence addresses how the definition varies across NASA Centers or Center-specific handbooks.

value.text: NASA defines systems engineering as "a methodical, multi-disciplinary approach for the design, realization, technical management, operations, and retirement of a system," where a system combines hardware, software, equipment, facilities, personnel, processes and procedures that together produce the capability needed to meet a need. It is also the art and science of developing an operable system capable of meeting requirements within often opposed constraints: a holistic, integrative discipline that balances structural, electrical, power, mechanism and human factors contributions into a coherent whole not dominated by any single discipline. The discipline therefore covers broadly the full life cycle, from mission and system concept definition, system-level requirements and technology development, through preliminary design, technical management, integration and verification, to operations and retirement. Systems engineering is about tradeoffs and compromises, using a broad crosscutting "big picture" view of the system rather than a single-discipline view.

issues: No draft or final report was supplied with this task, so there is nothing to check against the evidence and no claims to trace.
The question ('what NASA means by systems engineering and what broad activities it covers') is left unanswered, making the deliverable truncated.

Even the evidence base only supports the definitional half of the question: doc_30e20599232c112f gives NASA's definition and doc_137cce744dca38e2/doc_7671315dd147933b give general characterizations, but no retrieved source enumerates the broad activities (e.g., the SE engine phases from doc_fe1021f0925e93b2 alone are a partial, phase-level listing rather than a stated scope of the discipline).

value.answer: NASA defines systems engineering as "a methodical, multi-disciplinary approach for the design, realization, technical management, operations, and retirement of a system," where a system combines hardware, software, equipment, facilities, personnel, processes and procedures that together produce the capability needed to meet a need. It is also the art and science of developing an operable system capable of meeting requirements within often opposed constraints: a holistic, integrative discipline that balances structural, electrical, power, mechanism and human factors contributions into a coherent whole not dominated by any single discipline. The discipline therefore covers broadly the full life cycle, from mission and system concept definition, system-level requirements and technology development, through preliminary design, technical management, integration and verification, to operations and retirement. key_points: NASA defines systems engineering as a methodical, multi-disciplinary approach covering design, realization, technical management, operations and retirement of a system.
A system is the combination of elements—hardware, software, equipment, facilities, personnel, processes and procedures—that together provide the capability to meet a need.
Systems engineering is a holistic, integrative discipline that balances many engineering disciplines into a coherent whole not dominated by one perspective.
Broad activities span the full life cycle: concept definition, system-level requirements, technology development, preliminary design, technical management, integration, operations and retirement.
The discipline is fundamentally about tradeoffs and compromises, taking a crosscutting "big picture" view rather than a single-discipline view.

citations.quote_or_summary: At NASA, "systems engineering" is defined as a methodical, multi-disciplinary approach for the design, realization, technical management, operations, and retirement of a system; a system is the combination of elements that function together to produce the capability required to meet a need, including hardware, software, equipment, facilities, personnel, processes and procedures.

Systems engineering is the art and science of developing an operable system capable of meeting requirements within often opposed constraints; it is a holistic, integrative discipline balancing contributions of many disciplines to produce a coherent whole not dominated by a single discipline.
Systems engineering is about tradeoffs and compromises; it uses a broad crosscutting view of the system rather than a single discipline view, looking at the "big picture."
